whyVote.title: Politics shapes daily life whether you vote or not
whyVote.body: Governments set rules and budgets that affect tax, housing, health care, education, justice, and immigration. Those decisions apply to enrolled citizens and residents whether or not they cast a ballot. Skipping the vote does not pause Parliament or freeze policy.

whyVote.title: If you do not vote, others still decide who sits
whyVote.body: Seats in Parliament are filled from the votes that are cast. Not voting does not leave your share of power vacant for later — it simply means the people who did vote have a larger say over who forms government and which bills pass.

whyVote.title: Low turnout can make a minority of adults look like a majority of votes
whyVote.body: Imagine 100 enrolled electors and about 30 do not vote (30% non-turnout), so 70 ballots are counted. If a party or bloc wins 51% of those ballots, that is about 36 of the 70 votes cast — a majority of votes cast, but only about 36% of all enrolled electors. Seat allocation under MMP is based on votes cast (subject to threshold rules), not on the full enrolled or adult population. Majority of votes cast is not the same as majority of the population.

whyVote.title: Practical next steps
whyVote.body: Check you are enrolled, note election and advance-voting dates, and use official vote.nz guidance for how to cast a valid ballot. This site helps you compare parties; it does not tell you who to vote for.

history.title: Representative government begins
history.summary: The New Zealand Constitution Act 1852 created an elected House of Representatives. The first general election ran from mid-1853. The franchise was limited mainly to men who met property qualifications — a start of elected representation, not universal adult suffrage.

history.title: Maori seats created
history.summary: The Maori Representation Act 1867 established four Maori electorates so Maori men over 21 could vote and stand without the same individual freehold property hurdles that blocked many from general seats. The seats were meant as temporary special representation and later became a lasting feature of the system.

history.title: Male franchise widens
history.summary: Late-nineteenth-century reforms removed most remaining property barriers for adult men in general electorates, moving New Zealand toward near-universal male suffrage before women won the vote.

history.title: Women win the parliamentary vote
history.summary: On 19 September 1893 the Electoral Act gave women — including wahine Maori — the right to vote in parliamentary elections. New Zealand became the first self-governing country to enshrine women's parliamentary suffrage in law. Women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.

history.title: First-past-the-post era
history.summary: Almost all general elections used first-past-the-post (FPP): each voter had one vote in an electorate, and the candidate with the most votes won that seat. Party seat shares in Parliament often differed sharply from nationwide vote shares. A short second-ballot experiment ran around 1908-1913 before FPP returned.

history.title: Voters choose MMP
history.summary: An indicative referendum in 1992 and a binding referendum alongside the 1993 election asked New Zealanders to choose between FPP and mixed-member proportional (MMP). A majority supported MMP (about 54% in the 1993 binding vote), triggering a new electoral law for the next election.

history.title: First MMP election
history.summary: Voters cast a party vote and an electorate vote. List seats top up party representation toward proportionality (with threshold rules). The 1996 Parliament was more multiparty and demographically diverse than late-FPP Houses. Today's two-vote MMP system still uses that design — see About for the 5% threshold and electorate seat path.

myths.myth: A party vote for a smaller party is a wasted vote
myths.response: Under MMP the party vote mainly decides how many seats each party gets in Parliament. If a party reaches about 5% of the nationwide party vote, or wins an electorate seat, it can win list MPs — that is proportional representation, not first-past-the-post winner-takes-all. Honest caveat: a party vote for a party that finishes below the threshold and wins no electorate does not elect list MPs; that is how the published threshold works, not a reason to treat every non-major vote as pointless. See About for the 5% rule and electorate path.

You cast two votes. The electorate vote chooses a local MP. The party vote is the main driver of each party's overall seat share. Focusing only on the electorate race underuses the proportional half of the system that MMP was designed around.

myths.myth: You must vote for a big party or government will not form
myths.response: Under MMP, governments are often coalitions or confidence-and-supply arrangements, not single-party majorities. Parties that clear the threshold or hold seats can shape who forms government and which policies get through — even when they are not the largest party. Your party vote is about who you want in Parliament, not only who you guess will lead alone.

myths.myth: My single ballot cannot change anything
myths.response: Close electorate races and list-seat allocations are decided by margins. When turnout is lower, each ballot that is cast has more weight among the votes that fill seats. One vote is not a guarantee of a different outcome, but sitting out does not freeze Parliament — it leaves the decision to those who do vote.

myths.myth: Splitting your party and electorate votes is wrong or invalid
myths.response: Ticket-splitting — giving your party vote to one party and your electorate vote to a candidate from another — is a designed feature of MMP. Both votes count when cast correctly on a valid ballot. Official guidance explains how to mark the two votes; splitting them does not cancel your ballot.
